entry.content:
Links: dennisforbes.ca | lobsters | hacker news

Developer Dennis Forbes encountered a severe performance regression when inserting large JSON datasets into SQLite via a Rust service, with operations taking minutes instead of milliseconds. The bottleneck was traced to CPU-bound string tokenization during cross-platform compilation using Zig's `cc` compiler.

The slowdown originated from a pure-Zig replacement of standard C library string functions like `strspn` within Zig's libc implementation. Unlike standard library versions, the rewritten function repeatedly measures the entire length of the string on each iteration, creating a quadratic complexity trap that dramatically degrades tokenization performance on large files.

entry.title: `kill(1)` Parsing Bugs in `procps` Impact Ubuntu LTS Releases
entry.content:
Links: alangrow.com | lobsters | hacker news

Multiple Ubuntu LTS releases, from version 14.04 to 24.04, have contained bugs in the `kill(1)` command within the `procps` package. These issues stem from the use of `getopt` for command-line parsing, which causes negative process group identifiers (pgids) to be incorrectly interpreted as unrecognized options. In some cases, this misparsing leads to signals being sent to all processes on a machine except for PID 1.

Four distinct bugs were identified where previous attempts to fix parsing errors introduced new issues like segmentation faults or unintended shell termination. Because `kill` arguments can function as either signal names, numbers, or PIDs, `getopt`'s handling of option bundling is problematic for this utility. Positional argument parsing, similar to the implementation in FreeBSD, is recommended to ensure more predictable behavior.

entry.title: The Origins and Early Development of BSD Unix
entry.content:
Links: fosscomics.com | hacker news

In the late 1970s, Bill Joy and researchers at UC Berkeley created the Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) by bundling a Pascal compiler, line editors, and other utilities as an add-on package for AT&T Unix. By distributing these tools at cost, Berkeley fostered a tradition of sharing that helped spread Unix throughout universities and research institutions.

Following the release of the expanded 2BSD distribution, the acquisition of a VAX computer at Berkeley led graduate student Ozalp Babaoglu and Bill Joy to add virtual memory support to Unix 32/V. Their work culminated in 3BSD in December 1979, drawing the interest of DARPA and laying the groundwork for Unix's widespread adoption in government-funded research.

entry.title: Avoid Public Functions Calling Other Public Functions
entry.content:
Links: matklad.github.io | lobsters

When developing software modules, developers should avoid having public functions call other public functions to satisfy the DRY principle. This practice creates tension between designing an interface convenient for external callers and one easy to reuse internally, often leading to interface degradation and bloated optional parameters.

Instead, developers should extract shared implementation logic into a private helper function that both public functions can call. An exception to this rule applies to shortcut APIs, where public functions are intentionally defined as chains of calls to other public functions to serve as genuine shortcuts.

entry.title: The Kluever Maneuver for Two-Commit Bug Fixes
entry.content:

The Kluever Maneuver is a software development practice that splits a bug fix into two distinct commits: the first introduces a failing test that exposes the bug, while the second applies the fix and updates the test to pass. This structured approach ensures continuous integration passes at every commit and avoids false confidence from tests that might inadvertently pass before a fix is implemented.

By separating the demonstration of failure from the fix itself, developers gain verifiable proof that their code changes actually resolved the targeted issue. The technique also helps maintain clear version control histories and allows developers to easily link initial test commits directly to bug tracking systems.

Developer Drew Breunig has released Nesformer, a project that compiles a complete Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) 6502 CPU, 2 KB of RAM, and cartridge program ROM directly into the weights of a stock Qwen3.5 language model. Rather than being trained via machine learning, every parameter and state matrix is computed by a compiler, allowing the model to play games like Super Mario Bros. by predicting CPU execution tokens one at a time.

Building upon previous work like Qwenputer, Nesformer utilizes the model's Gated DeltaNet state matrices to function as the machine's memory while a host program handles peripheral tasks such as scanline rendering and controller input. While running significantly slower than real hardware—taking several seconds per frame—the system successfully executes NROM-compatible ROMs and achieves execution traces identical to conventional 6502 emulators.

entry.title: Analysis of Switch Statement Lowering in GCC
entry.content:
Links: xoranth.net | lobsters | hacker news

GCC implements `switch` statements using several distinct strategies depending on the distribution and density of case labels. For dense integer values, the compiler typically generates jump tables for efficient dispatching. When case values are sparse, GCC often utilizes a decision tree composed of comparison instructions, and in some instances, uses bitset-based tests for specific bit patterns.

The compiler employs specific heuristics to decide between these methods, such as evaluating the profitability of a jump table based on the number of required comparisons versus table size. Implementation details within the `pass_lower_switch` pass reveal that GCC uses dynamic programming to optimize bitset clusters and analyzes case ranges to determine the most efficient machine code.
